report.polishedVersion: At WDCC, where I volunteer, I worked on the Projects Health Dashboard, and I picked up a backfill script for the missing months of GitHub history. The old branches had been deleted, so I went through the PRs instead. I assumed a commit should count in the week its PR was merged. In the review, the tech lead pointed out that it should count in the week it was written. I switched to using each commit's own timestamp. Then I realized commits come in different states, so I raised that too, and we agreed to count all of them. It took two rounds of review and ten commits. Now I try to catch these problems before I open a PR.

report.polishedVersion: At New Oriental, we built a new marking dashboard on top of the backend's REST APIs. The biggest challenge was the response data: it was deeply nested and it changed often. In plain JavaScript we kept checking the API docs for field names, and we still made typos that only showed up in QA. So I set up openapi-typescript to generate types straight from the backend's Swagger spec. We worked design-first, so the spec was agreed before the endpoints were built. That meant I could build against the types while the backend team was still writing the API. Nobody wrote the API types by hand, and the editor gave us autocomplete for every field.

report.polishedVersion: The hardest problem I've solved was on the order page in our merchant console. Merchants said a competitor's console felt more responsive. I added code splitting, and LCP improved from about 3.5 seconds to 2.6 seconds, but the complaint was still there. When our team visited some merchants, I saw them run the same filter hundreds of times a day, reload the page, and keep several tabs open. That's when I realized I was measuring the wrong thing—the real problem was the same request being made again and again. Working with a senior engineer, I went through the request logs, and we implemented stale-while-revalidate caching in a Service Worker. A cached read came back in about 20 milliseconds, and the complaint went away.

report.polishedVersion: At ByteDance, we built a word cloud of the top keywords in video comments. When you hovered over a keyword, a tooltip showed its numbers, and inside that tooltip there was a second tooltip. I talked to the PM about it because the analysts needed to compare keywords, but if your mouse slipped, both tooltips would close, so you couldn't keep two open side by side. I didn't just say no — I suggested a modal so they could read and compare the details. The PM wanted the details close to the chart, so we met in the middle: we added a 'View details' link to the tooltip that opened the details in a panel next to the chart. I learned to advocate for the user's needs, not just my own preferences.

report.polishedVersion: I think breaking down a design into components is really important. First, I look at the overall design and try to understand its structure. Then I split it into components that make logical sense. I try to keep each component small and reusable, since reusable components are easier to maintain over time. I also consider how these components will interact with one another. Clear naming conventions matter too, so other developers can quickly understand the code. In general, I follow established best practices and aim to write clean, consistent code, though the right level of abstraction really depends on the project. Finally, staying in close communication with designers is important, since it helps ensure the components I build truly match their intended design.

report.polishedVersion: When I worked at ByteDance, I took on a requirement to implement a cloud chart with a tooltip. There was a second tooltip inside the first one, and when I hovered over the data, it only showed the comparison data, which was a bit unsuitable for the client. We had a discussion about it, and then I shared a new design with the PM that used a modal to show the comparison data. However, she thought it was too complicated. Through some trade-offs, we finally found a middle-ground design: a detail link that, when clicked, opened a panel on the side of the cloud chart. Reflection: I think we should focus more on how users can use the product comfortably, instead of just pushing our own 'best' design.
